​Public Comment Submission​
​Date: 06/15/2026​
​To: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human​
​Services​
​Attention: Docket ID: CMS-2026-1255​
​Reference: RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory Testing (Section III.E​
​of CMS-0062-P)​
​Submission Portal:​Regulations.gov​
​Re: Comment on the RFI for Prior Authorization and Access to Laboratory Testing​
​To Whom It May Concern:​
​I am writing on behalf of the Paltown Development Foundation, a nonprofit patient​
​advocacy organization that supports people affected by colorectal cancer and their​
​caregivers through its online patient communities. We are asking CMS to protect cancer​
​patients from the delays and denials that rigid prior authorization creates for medically​
​necessary laboratory and biomarker testing, where timely molecular results often decide​
​which treatment a patient gets.​
​We appreciate CMS's work to modernize and streamline prior authorization, and we​
​welcome the chance to respond to the RFI on access to laboratory testing in Section III.E.​
​In cancer care, timing is clinical, not administrative. Biomarker results decide which​
​treatment a patient starts, when therapy should change, how recurrence is caught, and​
​whether someone qualifies for a clinical trial. These tests are ordered for one of two​
​reasons: to read the genetic makeup of a tumor so it can be matched to the targeted​
​therapy or immunotherapy most likely to work, or to re-test a cancer that has changed​
​under treatment and grown resistant, so the next therapy fits the mutations that have​
​emerged. The evidence is consistent: waiting on biomarker results delays treatment​
​decisions,​[1]​​and the professional benchmark of reporting 90% of results within ten​
​working days of the sample reaching the lab​[2]​​is routinely missed because of paperwork,​
​not science. When a plan demands approval on or before the exact day the specimen is​
​collected, good samples get delayed, rejected, or thrown out even though the patient, the​
​doctor, and the lab all did everything right. The result is repeat blood draws, later​
​diagnoses, and delayed cancer care.​
​This falls hardest on the people least able to absorb it. For a rural, low-income,​
​immunocompromised, or seriously ill patient, a repeat draw is not a minor errand; it​
​means more time off work, more travel and childcare costs, and more physical strain in​
​__________________________________​
​PALTOWN.org​ ​|   A 501(c)3 corporation  |   EIN: 81-4532089​ ​|  410.849.9660  |​
​contact@paltown.org​
​the middle of treatment. A billing technicality should never outweigh documented​
​medical need.​
​The pattern of harm is well documented. In a survey of more than 300 oncology​
​providers, 66% said insurer coverage and prior-authorization rules are a moderate or​
​significant barrier to appropriate biomarker testing, even though 91% rely on clinical​
​guidelines to decide what to order.​[3]​​Laboratory tests inform roughly 70% of all medical​
​decisions, and denials or delays for these tests can have life-threatening consequences.​[4]​
​The three scenarios below, all realistic in everyday colorectal cancer (CRC) care, show​
​what that looks like in practice.​
​Scenario 1: an out-of-date rule blocks a test that was done right. Someone in their early​
​50s is newly diagnosed with advanced colorectal cancer. Before choosing treatment, their​
​oncologist orders a single test that reads several tumor genes at once, the standard way to​
​find out which treatments will actually work. The sample is handled perfectly, but the​
​insurer's system denies it automatically because its rules still assume older,​
​one-gene-at-a-time testing.​[5]​​To avoid losing time, the oncologist starts standard​
​chemotherapy while they wait on approval. Over the next few weeks the patient misses​
​workdays and develops a common chemo side effect: lasting nerve damage in the hands​
​and feet. When the test is finally approved, it confirms that a gentler targeted therapy​
​would have worked better from the start, but the nerve damage is permanent.​
​Scenario 2: same cancer, two very different outcomes. Two patients have the same stage​
​IV colorectal cancer and need the same comprehensive gene test. The first is treated at a​
​large academic center whose prior-authorization team gets the full panel approved. It​
​turns up an uncommon but treatable change, a HER2-positive (HER2+) result, that the​
​basic test isn't designed to detect; the patient is matched to a targeted therapy, responds​
​well, and gets back to normal life. The second goes to a two-doctor rural clinic with no​
​staff to fight insurers. The comprehensive panel is denied, so the oncologist runs the​
​narrower test the plan will cover. It looks only for the most common genetic changes,​
​which do not include HER2, comes back "nothing found," and the treatable change is​
​never caught. That patient gets chemotherapy alone, never learns a targeted option​
​existed, and the cancer keeps growing.​[5]​​Same disease, same biology, but only the​
​patient whose clinic could out-argue the insurer got the better medicine. This lands​
​hardest on the small and rural clinics that disproportionately serve low-income and​
​minority patients, widening cancer disparities instead of closing them.​
​Scenario 3: a delay becomes the difference between life and death. A patient has an​
​aggressive, fast-growing colorectal cancer. Its features, a right-sided tumor with poorly​
​differentiated cells, lead the oncologist to strongly suspect a BRAF V600E mutation,​
​which now has a targeted drug combination that can hold it back and works far better for​
​these tumors than chemotherapy alone. The oncologist orders the test to confirm it, but​
​approval stalls; the result takes weeks, and the lab holds off running it because it risks not​
​being paid.​[4]​​Meanwhile the patient stays on a weaker regimen, the cancer keeps​
​advancing, and they grow weaker, until by the time the test is approved and confirms the​
​__________________________________​
​PALTOWN.org​ ​|   A 501(c)3 corporation  |   EIN: 81-4532089​ ​|  410.849.9660  |​
​contact@paltown.org​
​mutation, they are too sick to safely receive the therapy that could have helped. For​
​aggressive disease, weeks lost to paperwork are not administrative. They can be decisive.​
​These are not edge cases. They are the predictable result of applying prior authorization​
​to standard, guideline-recommended cancer testing, where it does little to protect quality​
​and mostly just delays the care patients need.​[5]​
​We urge CMS to keep prior authorization for the few cases where it is genuinely​
​necessary and to drop it where it has become an administrative barrier rather than a real​
​safeguard. Five federal priorities should guide that line.​
​CMS should require health plans to:​
​1. ​Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected.
​2. ​Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.
​3. ​Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available.
​4. ​Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.
​5. ​Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative.
​In addition, plans should be open about their decision criteria, denial reasons, and​
​performance by specialty, and should be accountable when a denial stems from outdated​
​policy that no longer reflects current medical and scientific evidence. That transparency​
​lets patients, clinicians, and CMS see where the process works and where it breaks, and​
​holds insurers to the same evidence standards that clinicians must meet.​[4]​
​These costs do not disappear; they grow. When prior authorization delays the right test,​
​patients start the wrong treatment or none at all, decline faster, and reach harder-to-treat​
​stages. The bill is both human and financial: more and longer hospital stays, earlier​
​palliative care, avoidable harm from the wrong therapy, lost income, and strain on​
​families. Much of it is preventable, and the administrative burden of prior authorization​
​on time-sensitive testing is a big part of why it happens. Fixing it is one of the clearest​
​chances CMS has to improve outcomes and lower costs at once.​
​Cancer patients need fast, uninterrupted access to biomarker results so that they and their​
​care teams can make informed, sometimes life-saving decisions. Prior authorization​
​should help that happen, not stand in the way.​
​Thank you for your consideration.​
​Sincerely,​
​
​Director of Operations & Finance; Interim Executive Director​
​Paltown Development Foundation​
​EIN: 81-4532089​
​Edgewater, MD 21037​

analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Paltown Development Foundation; signed by Director of Operations & Finance / Interim Executive Director.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** 501(c)(3) nonprofit patient advocacy organization supporting people affected by colorectal cancer and caregivers through online patient communities.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Paltown Development Foundation responds to the RFI on prior authorization and access to laboratory testing, urging CMS to protect cancer patients from delays and denials for medically necessary laboratory and biomarker testing. The commenter asks CMS to allow retroactive authorization after specimens are collected, prohibit timing-only denials, prevent repeat blood draws when valid specimens exist, require expedited oncology review, protect patients from surprise costs, and require transparency around criteria, denial reasons, and specialty performance.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** GENERAL; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; TRANSPARENCY.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** Section III.E of CMS-0062-P referenced; no CFR citations mentioned.
- **Standards referenced:** Colorectal cancer molecular biomarker testing guideline from ASCP/CAP/AMP/ASCO; no FHIR, NCPDP, or API implementation standards discussed directly.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Prior authorization barriers to oncology laboratory and biomarker testing**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Biomarker testing determines targeted therapy, immunotherapy, treatment changes, recurrence detection, resistance mutations, and clinical trial eligibility. Delays caused by PA paperwork can lead to wrong therapy, later diagnosis, disease progression, repeat blood draws, and lost treatment opportunities.
- **Specific request:** CMS should keep PA only where genuinely necessary and remove it where it functions as an administrative barrier to standard, guideline-recommended cancer testing.

**Topic 2: Retroactive authorization and timing-based denials**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL / PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Plans that require approval by the specimen collection date can cause valid samples to be delayed, rejected, or discarded, even when the patient, clinician, and lab acted correctly.
- **Specific request:** Require plans to allow retroactive authorization after specimen collection and prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.

**Topic 3: Avoiding repeat blood draws and administrative rework**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Repeat draws impose travel, childcare, work, financial, and physical burdens, especially for rural, low-income, immunocompromised, seriously ill, and cancer patients undergoing treatment.
- **Specific request:** Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available.

**Topic 4: Expedited review for oncology diagnostics and biomarker testing**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS / GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** In aggressive cancers, weeks lost to paperwork can determine whether a patient remains healthy enough to receive targeted therapy.
- **Specific request:** Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.

**Topic 5: Patient financial protections**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** Patients should not face surprise costs when delays are administrative and outside their control.
- **Specific request:** Protect patients from surprise costs and coverage denials caused by administrative PA delays.

**Topic 6: Transparency and accountability**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS / API-USAGE-METRICS / TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Support/expand.
- **Rationale:** Patients, clinicians, and CMS need visibility into where PA processes fail, especially when denials rely on outdated criteria inconsistent with current science.
- **Specific request:** Require plans to be transparent about decision criteria, denial reasons, performance by specialty, and accountability when policy is outdated.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S16/S17:** The comment calls for clear denial reasons and prohibits denial based only on PA timing when medical necessity is documented.
- **S20/S43:** Responds indirectly by requesting expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing where delay can affect treatment decisions and survival.
- **S29/S35:** Recommends transparency and performance reporting by specialty to identify payer barriers, outdated policies, and process failures.
- **S66-S82:** Directly responds to the RFI on prior authorization and access to laboratory testing in Section III.E, emphasizing biomarker/genomic testing protections for colorectal cancer.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Allow retroactive authorization when specimens have already been collected.
2. Prohibit denials based solely on authorization timing.
3. Prevent unnecessary repeat blood draws when a valid specimen is available.
4. Require expedited review for oncology-related diagnostic and biomarker testing.
5. Protect patients from surprise costs when delays are administrative.
6. Require plan transparency around decision criteria, denial reasons, and performance by specialty.
7. Hold plans accountable when denials stem from outdated policies that no longer reflect current medical and scientific evidence.
8. Keep prior authorization only for cases where it is genuinely necessary and eliminate it where it delays guideline-recommended cancer testing.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Rigid PA timing rules, outdated payer policies, delayed biomarker results, repeat blood draws, surprise costs, and lack of transparency.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Later diagnoses, delayed cancer care, wrong initial therapy, permanent chemotherapy side effects, missed targeted therapy opportunities, clinical trial ineligibility, disease progression, palliative care, hospitalizations, lost income, family strain, and widened disparities.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Insurer systems that assume outdated one-gene testing; lack of rural clinic staff to fight denials; labs holding tests because of payment risk; payer requirements that authorization be complete on or before specimen collection.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Professional benchmark that 90% of colorectal cancer molecular biomarker results should be reported within ten working days of lab receipt; survey of more than 300 oncology providers found 66% view insurer coverage and PA rules as a moderate/significant barrier to appropriate biomarker testing; 91% rely on clinical guidelines to decide what to order; laboratory tests inform roughly 70% of medical decisions.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Annals of Oncology article on biomarker results delaying treatment decisions; ASCP/CAP/AMP/ASCO colorectal cancer molecular biomarker testing guideline; ACS CAN survey of payer coverage policies for tumor biomarker and pharmacogenomic testing; American Clinical Laboratory Association 2024 PA reform recommendations; Binaytara article on insurance barriers to genomic testing.
- **Examples provided:** Advanced CRC patient denied comprehensive testing by outdated rules; two stage IV CRC patients with different outcomes depending on academic center vs rural clinic PA capacity; BRAF V600E suspected aggressive CRC patient whose approval delay means targeted therapy arrives too late.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Colorectal cancer patients, caregivers, oncology providers, rural clinics, low-income patients, immunocompromised and seriously ill patients, laboratories, health plans, CMS, and patient advocacy organizations.
- **Economic implications:** Delays increase costs through wrong therapy, hospital stays, palliative care, lost income, family strain, repeat testing, and later-stage disease care.
- **Technical feasibility:** The comment does not address FHIR/API feasibility; it focuses on policy guardrails that align PA timing with lab workflows.
- **Patient care impact:** Very high; biomarker testing can determine treatment selection, targeted therapy eligibility, resistance mutations, trial eligibility, and survival-related treatment timing.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Concerned and reform-oriented; supportive of CMS modernization but opposed to rigid PA barriers for cancer testing.
- **Tone:** Patient-centered, urgent, evidence-based, and critical of outdated payer policies.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "In cancer care, timing is clinical, not administrative." - Context: Core argument that biomarker testing delays affect treatment decisions.
2. "A billing technicality should never outweigh documented medical need." - Context: Objection to timing-based specimen collection denials.
3. "Same disease, same biology, but only the patient whose clinic could out-argue the insurer got the better medicine." - Context: Rural/academic center disparity scenario.
4. "Prior authorization should help that happen, not stand in the way." - Context: Conclusion on fast access to biomarker results.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - The comment focuses on expedited review and timely lab results, though not on rule compliance dates.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Surprise costs, repeat draws, lost income, hospitalizations, wrong therapy, and family strain are central concerns.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Rural/small clinics lacking staff to fight insurers and labs facing payment risk are highlighted.
- [ ] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Not addressed.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - The comment stresses rural, low-income, minority, immunocompromised, and seriously ill patients disproportionately affected by PA barriers.
- [ ] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Not addressed from an API/standards perspective.
- [ ] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Not addressed, aside from clinical biomarker testing guidelines.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - The primary theme is timely access to medically necessary lab and biomarker testing.
- [ ] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Not addressed.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The comment implicitly involves patients, doctors, labs, and plans, but coordination is secondary.
- [ ] **MEDICAL-VS-PHARMACY-BENEFIT** - Not addressed.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Requests openness about decision criteria, denial reasons, performance by specialty, and outdated policies.
- [ ] **SMALL-PAYER-IMPACT** - Not addressed.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Strong focus on real-world specimen collection, lab processing, and PA timing workflows.
- [ ] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - Not addressed.
